cells.tense: You are here, at the private edge of what you can see clearly.
cells.act: keep building the thing with sustained craft
cells.ask: Name whatever you watch most closely, and keep coming back to it through the week. It deepens at the pace you set, not the pace anyone else would set for you.
cells.core:
You've been refining something no one else can see yet — sorting what matters from what doesn't, on purpose, alone. That isn't a side activity. When a hard call comes, the ground under it has already been laid, and it holds because you laid it slowly. What this balance asks is for you to treat that as work.

So keep at the one private practice you chose, at the pace you set, and let today's part be today's part. Skill like this doesn't come from a push; it comes from showing up again tomorrow and the day after, with the same quiet attention. What you can now tell apart in an instant used to be a blur. That was built, over time, and it keeps building as long as you keep turning toward it.

cells.place: In the knowing that comes before the analysis

cells.tense: You will have refined it long before anyone could possibly hear it.
cells.act: accept the acknowledgment when it comes
cells.ask: Let one person hear a line of what you've been working out before it's polished — out loud, without taking it back. Then let whatever they say land.
cells.core:
You can see the shape of a thing before anyone else can, and by the time it's said the version they get has already been smoothed past where they were. From your side that's care; from theirs a position arrives fully formed and nobody watched you build it. That's how it bends when it's running ahead.

So let one person in on the rough part — a sentence, not the whole case, and not the tidied one. Then accept what comes back, even if it's only a nod. What you can see isn't given away by being seen; it enters the room where somebody can actually use it. The version you let them hold will be coarser than the one in your head, and something real can start from it.

cells.tense: You were someone who could tell what mattered, and you have not been back there.
cells.act: accept what is offered for what you gave
cells.ask: Someone still owes you a fair return for something you worked out for them. Take it this time — one favour, one answer, one thing they offer — and don't hurry to hand it back.
cells.core:
A door you were standing in front of is already behind you. You used to take a thing apart until you could see what it was made of — an offer, a decision, a person. Somewhere along the way the taking-apart stopped, and you've been waiting for a sign that it's worth starting again.

What's thin isn't the sharpness; it's the exchange. Somebody out there still holds something they mean to give you back, and you've been waving it off. Take it this time. Let the return come at its own size, whichever size that is, and don't rush to even it out. Attention that goes only one way runs down. Fair give and take is where this one refills from, and it refills from outside.
cells.sheetLine: Take back the fair return you keep waving off.

cells.tense: You are already making the private call before anyone has asked the question.
cells.act: let the satisfaction of a finished thing land
cells.ask: Choose something you finished and sit with it for an hour, satisfied. Don't sharpen it or extend it. Walk through the room you made and leave every object where it is.
cells.core:
The private call is already happening — you catch the difference between what matters and what doesn't before a word is said — and you've been telling yourself it doesn't count, or that anyone would do the same. Nobody hands out credit for a thing that happens this quietly, so none comes. That's the shape you're in.

Underneath it there's something simpler: your eye is mostly about endings. You spot where a matter finishes as clearly as where it starts, and then you move straight to the next one. So finish differently once. Sit for an hour with something already done and take in the satisfaction of it — yours, not the person it was for, not the improved version. What got made, your eyes made it. That's the shorter way back.
cells.sheetLine: Let what you noticed and finished belong to you.

attempts.check: The one unsupported claim: I have rendered the Too Much cell's surrounding people as tiring of the private work — the record shows no such evidence, only the projection ahead of timing. The reader could reasonably say they aren't doing the noticing on anyone's behalf and that their private analysis does not burden anyone; stripped of that addition, the cell's task survives because it hands the noticing back to them alone in the seat. The sentence that serves me more than them is any clause about what the work costs the people around them — cut. The Too Little ask survives being wrong because it stands as a fact rather than a demand: if no someone is absent, the noticing still releases the seat to the person's own reclaimed attention. The Too Much ask survives because visibility of one's own private work is always available to the person regardless of who is watching, and the honoring does not require the honored act to land. The Unacknowledged ask survives because the hour of a finished thing requires nothing but the person and the thing.
